<section id="overview" class="content-section">

## What is Eduardo Telles Gi Octopus Guard System?

**The Eduardo Telles Gi Octopus Guard System is a study framework for connecting octopus sweeps and back takes while accounting for gi grips.**

A gi grip can change both the available entry and the response to a sweep. Eduardo Telles's Octopus With Pajamas gives this guide a specific gi focus, linking half-guard and closed-guard situations with butterfly-assisted movement and back exposure. Use that narrower brief when comparing it with Craig Jones's no-gi Octopus guide. The aim here is to recognise a few repeatable choices in your existing guard, rather than collect every variation at once.

The sequence and drills below are original BJJGraph study suggestions, not a course transcript or an official instructor curriculum. Use the linked demonstrations for technical detail, then compare one selected lesson with a controlled partner round.

</section>

<section id="key-principles" class="content-section">

## Core Principles
- The sleeve contact depends on clothing and changes the available connection; it cannot be copied unchanged into no-gi.
- The posting choice changes your base and helps explain how the movement is supported.
- The partner response may expose their back, but that exposure must still be connected to stable rear control.
- Both partners should understand the starting contact and intended direction of movement.
- Their grips and body constraints differ, so success in one entry does not show the other is reliable.
- Whether the new top position is controlled or the partner can recover before the transition is complete.


</section>

<section id="key-components" class="content-section">

## Key Components
**Choose a familiar gi guard** (Give the choose a familiar gi guard stage a concrete objective before connecting it to the next exchange.)
Start from half guard with agreed grips and identify where the overback connection becomes available.

**Compare the posting options** (Give the compare the posting options stage a concrete objective before connecting it to the next exchange.)
Practise the basic sweep and its elbow-post variation separately, noticing how each changes your base.

**Read the sweep defense** (Give the read the sweep defense stage a concrete objective before connecting it to the next exchange.)
Allow one defensive post and decide whether the back is available or whether the sweep needs to be reset.

**Connect a butterfly option** (Give the connect a butterfly option stage a concrete objective before connecting it to the next exchange.)
Introduce the butterfly-assisted branch only when both partners can identify the direction of the intended movement.

**Transfer to closed guard** (Give the transfer to closed guard stage a concrete objective before connecting it to the next exchange.)
Study how the sleeve-grip entry changes the same decision and compare it with the original half-guard round.



</section>

<section id="implementation-sequence" class="content-section">

## Implementation Sequence
1. **Choose a familiar gi guard**: Start from half guard with agreed grips and identify where the overback connection becomes available.


2. **Compare the posting options**: Practise the basic sweep and its elbow-post variation separately, noticing how each changes your base.


3. **Read the sweep defense**: Allow one defensive post and decide whether the back is available or whether the sweep needs to be reset.


4. **Connect a butterfly option**: Introduce the butterfly-assisted branch only when both partners can identify the direction of the intended movement.


5. **Transfer to closed guard**: Study how the sleeve-grip entry changes the same decision and compare it with the original half-guard round.




</section>

<section id="common-obstacles" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## What Challenges Will You Face?
- **Using the gi lesson as a no-gi grip prescription**: Identify which contact depends on clothing before attempting to transfer the drill.
- **Adding a roll before understanding the base**: Return to the basic sweep and practise the change of weight cooperatively.
- **Ignoring the partner after the sweep**: Continue only far enough to establish top control or identify the back exposure.
- **Treating two entry positions as identical**: Record the half-guard and closed-guard results separately.


</section>

<section id="assessment-metrics" class="content-section">

## How to Measure Your Progress
**Starting-position recognition**: Check whether the practitioner can describe the relevant control from Half Guard.
Proficiency indicators:
- Names the starting position
- Identifies the first useful contact
- Explains why the chosen lesson fits this exchange


**Reaction recognition**: Assess the decision when the partner stops the first option.
Proficiency indicators:
- Names the defensive response
- Pauses at the point the original option is lost
- Chooses a supported continuation or reset


**Endpoint quality**: Review the position reached after the selected movement.
Proficiency indicators:
- Can name the intended endpoint
- Checks the partner still has an escape response
- Separates a transient opening from sustained control


**Practice transfer**: Compare the same task as agreed resistance and partner reactions change.
Proficiency indicators:
- Repeats the starting conditions
- Records the first point of failure
- Chooses one specific adjustment for the next round




</section>

<section id="training-methodology" class="content-section hide-minimal">

## How to Train This System Effectively

### Drilling Approach
BJJGraph practice suggestion: start from Half Guard and give the partner one agreed response. Work through the first two stages cooperatively, then stop each repetition at the chosen control or recovery endpoint. Add another reaction only when both partners can explain what changed. Keep submission entries controlled and release immediately on a tap or request to stop. Review the lost connection before adding speed.

### Progression Path
**Recognise** (Focus: Start from half guard with agreed grips and identify where the overback connection becomes available.)
**Rehearse** (Focus: Practise the basic sweep and its elbow-post variation separately, noticing how each changes your base.)
**Respond** (Focus: Allow one defensive post and decide whether the back is available or whether the sweep needs to be reset.)
**Connect** (Focus: Study how the sleeve-grip entry changes the same decision and compare it with the original half-guard round.)


### Common Mistakes
- Using the gi lesson as a no-gi grip prescription
- Adding a roll before understanding the base
- Ignoring the partner after the sweep
- Treating two entry positions as identical


</section>
